clue.text: Trapped without spades or clubs

parts.note: a player whose hand holds no black suits has only hearts and diamonds, so the hand is all red; caught with such a hand is the playful second reading of being seized in the act

explanation.walkthrough: Spades and clubs are the black suits in a pack of cards, so a hand without them holds only red cards.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means seized in the very act of wrongdoing, which is what being trapped suggests.

clue.text: Jeer during trial in the cookhouse

indicators.note: the jeer comes during the trial, so its word sits inside the word for the trial

parts.note: a trial is a court case
to boo is to jeer

explanation.surface: Someone is heckled at a hearing held in a kitchen.
explanation.definitionFit: A caboose is a ship's galley, the kitchen on deck, so a cookhouse in naval usage.

clue.text: Acceptable and wise custom

parts.note: U means upper-class and so socially acceptable, a long-standing British label
a sage person is wise

explanation.surface: A tradition is praised as both proper and sensible.
explanation.walkthrough: U as 'acceptable' comes from the 1950s British split of usage into U (upper-class) and non-U.
explanation.definitionFit: Usage is established practice or habit, a synonym of custom.

clue.text: Top-quality sixth form

definitions.meaning: in British schools the sixth form is the senior, highest year group, read as the highest class

explanation.walkthrough: The sixth form is the final two years of British secondary school, so it is the 'high class' in the building.
explanation.definitionFit: Superior in grade or standing, and jokingly the topmost class in a school.

clue.text: Note lack of faith in last retreat

parts.note: re is the second note of the sol-fa scale
doubt is an absence of belief or trust

explanation.surface: Losing belief, someone seeks a final refuge.
explanation.definitionFit: A redoubt is a fortified stronghold, a place defenders fall back to as a final refuge.

clue.text: Crack appearing in the German fishing boat

indicators.note: the crack shows up within the German article, so one word goes inside the other

parts.note: der is a German word for the
a rift is a crack or split

explanation.surface: A split has opened in a trawler from Germany.
explanation.definitionFit: A drifter is a vessel that fishes with drift nets.

clue.text: Redcaps get stuck into the drink — plenty of it

indicators.note: the redcaps are pushed into the drink, putting one word inside the other

parts.note: ale is beer, a drink
redcaps is British slang for military police, abbreviated MP

explanation.surface: Military police tuck into the beer with no shortage of it.
explanation.walkthrough: Redcaps are British military police, named for their red caps.
explanation.definitionFit: Ample describes a generous amount, more than enough, which is plenty.

clue.text: They must be met by writers of obituaries

definitions.text: They must be met by writers of obituaries

parts.words: They must be met by writers of obituaries
parts.note: journalists must meet time limits, and obituary writers' lines are literally about dead people

explanation.definitionFit: Deadlines are cut-off times for copy, which writers of any kind must meet.

clue.text: Friendlier relations see portable home engulfed by river

indicators.note: the portable home is swallowed by the river, so it goes inside the river's name

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Britain
a tent is a home you can carry

explanation.surface: A camper watches a tent swept away by a river.
explanation.definitionFit: Détente is an easing of tension between states, a thaw in diplomatic hostility.

clue.text: Second-rate, tatty crew!

parts.note: B is the second grade, as in B-movie
ragged means shabby or tatty

explanation.surface: An insult hurled at a scruffy, inferior team of sailors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crew' is not a team here but the old past tense of crow, to boast.
explanation.definitionFit: Crew is a past form of crow, to boast loudly, so it matches boasted.

clue.text: Tissue graft I'm taking to the workshop

parts.note: taken as written without the apostrophe
a plant is a factory or workshop

explanation.surface: Someone carries a sample of grafted tissue to a factory.
explanation.definitionFit: Surgeons transplant living tissue into the body, which is an implant.

clue.text: Where a plaintiff may start to press his suit

parts.note: to open is to start
to court someone is to woo them, pressing one's suit

explanation.surface: A man begins pursuing his romantic proposal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press his suit' sounds like ironing, but pressing a suit is wooing; the definition is the place a plaintiff may sue.
explanation.definitionFit: Proceedings held publicly before a judge are the venue in which a litigant brings a case.

clue.text: She even pocketed two quid

indicators.note: the money is pocketed by the other word, so it goes inside it

parts.note: e'en is the poetic contraction of even
L is the abbreviation for a pound (quid in British slang), so two of them make LL

explanation.surface: A woman even managed to pocket a couple of pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: Quid is British slang for a pound, abbreviated L from Latin libra.
explanation.definitionFit: Ellen is a woman's name, so a female person referred to as she.

clue.text: Passage from a religious pamphlet

parts.note: ex is Latin for from, as in ex-works
a tract is a short religious leaflet

explanation.surface: A reading is taken out of a church leaflet.
explanation.definitionFit: An extract is an excerpt, a section quoted from a longer text.

clue.text: Difficult task for brotherhood of high standing

parts.note: standing high means tall
a religious or knightly order is a brotherhood

explanation.surface: A challenge is set for an exalted fraternity.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means a demanding request, one hard to fulfil.

clue.text: Soldiers rendezvous to offer funds

parts.note: RE are the Royal Engineers, British Army soldiers
a venue is a meeting place

explanation.surface: Troops meet up to provide money.
explanation.definitionFit: Revenue is income, money coming in to be spent.

clue.text: Clerics without much time in their homes

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside: the clerics wrap round the time

parts.note: vicars are clergymen
an age is a long time

explanation.surface: Churchmen with little time to spare stay at home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like 'lacking' but here means outside, its old sense; the definition's 'their' refers back to the clerics.
explanation.definitionFit: Vicarages are the houses provided for parish priests.

clue.text: Requests for visits

definitions.meaning: asks someone formally to do something

explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both appeals to someone and drops in on them.

clue.text: Abandoned thespian group on holiday

parts.note: the cast is the actors in a production
off work means on holiday

explanation.surface: Actors left stranded while away on vacation.
explanation.definitionFit: Cast-off things are discarded or rejected, as a deserted object is.

clue.text: Boa, perhaps, permitted to lie below cheek

indicators.note: in a down clue the permitted word is placed beneath the cheek word

parts.note: neck is British slang for cheek, impudence
let means allowed or permitted

explanation.surface: A snake is allowed to rest under someone's face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boa' is a snake on the surface, but a feather boa is worn round the throat; 'neck' as cheek is British slang for nerve.
explanation.definitionFit: A feather boa is one example of a small scarf-like wrap worn round the throat.

clue.text: Commonplace maxim, but with a cutting edge

parts.note: hack work is commonplace or trite
a saw is an old saying

explanation.surface: A trite proverb that is nonetheless sharp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutting edge' reads as sharp wit, but it is literal: the tool has a toothed blade.
explanation.definitionFit: A hacksaw is a tool whose toothed blade cuts metal.

clue.text: Valiance is more his style

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held 'Valiance is more his style' (7): 'is more his' is ten letters and no reading gives the seven of HEROISM; the anagram of IS MORE needs only an H, which no word supplies cleanly, so the clue is likely misprinted

clue.text: Awful weather in which to make a garland

indicators.note: awful weather is disordered, so the letters of weather are mixed up

explanation.surface: Someone braves a storm to weave flowers into a circlet.
explanation.definitionFit: To wreathe is to twist flowers or leaves into a ring.

clue.text: Termagant both sunny and chill

parts.note: S stands for sunny on weather charts
cold means chill

explanation.surface: A shrewish woman described as both warm and frosty.
explanation.definitionFit: A termagant is a nagging, quarrelsome woman, the same sense as the noun scold.

clue.text: Attract apprentice by affected articulation

parts.note: to draw is to attract
L is a learner, as on British learner-driver plates

explanation.surface: Someone lures a trainee with a put-on accent.
explanation.definitionFit: A drawl is slow, lengthened speech, often put on for effect.

clue.text: Shell left by a wagon on the crest

parts.note: a cart is a wagon
a ridge is the crest of a hill

explanation.surface: An empty casing is found where a wagon stood on a hilltop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shell' reads as a seashell, but it is ammunition.
explanation.definitionFit: A cartridge is a casing holding a charge and bullet, a kind of ammunition round.

clue.text: Tiny tot taken to a play

parts.note: a tot is a small measure of spirits, a dram

explanation.surface: A small child is taken to the theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tiny tot' looks like a small child but is a nip of whisky.
explanation.definitionFit: A drama is a work for the stage.

clue.text: Occasional dance proves bizarre

parts.note: odd means occasional, as in the odd visit
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: A once-in-a-while dance turns out strange.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as an adjective, oddball means eccentric or strange.

clue.text: 10 workaholics find pleasure there

definitions.meaning: refers to the answer at 10 across, a tissue graft
workaholics are happy deep in hard work, graft being British slang for toil

explanation.walkthrough: Graft is British slang for hard work, so being in it delights workaholics.
explanation.definitionFit: Ingraft is a variant spelling meaning to graft one tissue into another, the same as the earlier answer, and also reads as being in hard work.

clue.text: An expression of nostalgia

parts.note: a stock phrase people say when doing something in memory of the past

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is said when doing something in fond memory of earlier days.
